title: Network Devices
summary: Routers, switches, hubs — learn what each device does, which OSI layer it lives on, and when to use one over another.

blocks.markdown:
A **network device** is hardware that connects computers or segments of a network together.

- Each device works at a specific **OSI layer**, which determines how smart it is — can it read IP addresses? MAC addresses? Raw bits?
- Knowing the layer tells you what the device can and cannot do.
- The common devices: NIC, hub, repeater, bridge, switch, router, gateway, modem, wireless access point.

blocks.subTitle: Device at a glance
blocks.markdown:
Quick reference — device, OSI layer, and job.

| Device | OSI Layer | Job |
|---|---|---|
| Hub | 1 – Physical | Broadcast bits to all ports |
| Switch | 2 – Data Link | Forward frames by MAC address |
| Router | 3 – Network | Route packets by IP address |
| Bridge | 2 – Data Link | Connect two LAN segments |
| Gateway | 4–7 – Upper | Translate between protocols |
| Modem | 1 – Physical | Convert digital ↔ analog signal |
| WAP | 2 – Data Link | Wireless entry point to a LAN |
| Repeater | 1 – Physical | Amplify a signal over distance |

blocks.subTitle: NIC & repeater
blocks.markdown:
**Layer 1 (Physical)** devices deal only in raw bits — they have no awareness of addresses.

- **NIC (Network Interface Card)** — the hardware in your machine that sends and receives bits on a cable or over Wi-Fi. Every NIC has a unique **MAC address** burned in at the factory.
- **Repeater** — amplifies a weakening signal so it can travel further. No intelligence; it just boosts. Use it to extend a cable run beyond its distance limit.

blocks.subTitle: Hub
blocks.markdown:
A **hub** is a Layer 1 device that connects multiple machines in a star layout.

- When a frame arrives on any port, the hub copies it to **every other port** — it has no idea who the destination is.
- All machines share one **collision domain**: if two send at the same moment, signals collide and both must retry.
- Hubs are obsolete; switches replaced them in all modern networks.

blocks.subTitle: Bridge
blocks.markdown:
A **bridge** operates at Layer 2 (Data Link) and connects two separate LAN segments.

- It reads the **MAC address** of each frame to decide which segment to forward it to, or whether to block it.
- A **MAC address** (**Media Access Control**) is the hardware identifier of a NIC — 48 bits, written like `AA:BB:CC:DD:EE:FF`.
- Bridges reduced collisions by splitting a large network into two smaller collision domains.

blocks.subTitle: Switch
blocks.markdown:
A **switch** is a multi-port bridge — effectively a smarter hub that works at Layer 2.

- It builds a **MAC address table** (a map of which MAC lives on which port) by watching traffic.
- It sends each frame **only to the correct port**, so other ports stay quiet. Each port is its own collision domain.
- This is why switches replaced hubs: far less wasted bandwidth, no collisions.

See [physical-data-link-layer](physical-data-link-layer) for how frames are structured.

blocks.subTitle: Router
blocks.markdown:
A **router** operates at Layer 3 (Network) and connects **different networks** together.

- It reads the **IP address** in each packet and consults its **routing table** to decide the best path to the destination.
- Every packet that crosses the internet passes through multiple routers.
- A router creates a separate **broadcast domain** on each interface — broadcast traffic does not leak between networks.

See [routing](routing) for how routing tables are built.

The most-tested distinction in networking interviews.

- **Switch (L2)** — works within one network (LAN). Forwards by MAC. Fast, cheap. Cannot connect two different IP networks.
- **Router (L3)** — connects different networks. Forwards by IP. Handles internet routing and separates broadcast domains.

Rule of thumb: switch for **inside** the office network; router for **between** networks (office → internet).

blocks.subTitle: Multilayer switch
blocks.markdown:
A **multilayer switch** (sometimes called an L3 switch) can do both: it switches at Layer 2 for local traffic and routes at Layer 3 for inter-VLAN or WAN traffic.

- Used in large enterprise networks where you want routing speed without a separate dedicated router for every VLAN.
- It uses dedicated ASICs (chips) to route at wire speed — faster than a traditional router for high-volume local routing.
- A **VLAN** (Virtual LAN) is a logical segment of a switch that acts as its own network.

blocks.subTitle: Gateway & modem
blocks.markdown:
**Gateway** and **modem** handle protocol translation — not just forwarding.

- **Gateway (L4–L7)** — connects networks that speak different protocols. Example: an email gateway converts messages between SMTP and an older proprietary mail format. The term is loose; "default gateway" in IP networking usually just means the router for the local network.
- **Modem (L1)** — **mod**ulates and **dem**odulates: converts digital bits from your computer to analog signals for the phone/cable line, and back again. Your ISP modem sits between your home router and the internet.

blocks.subTitle: Wireless access point
blocks.markdown:
A **wireless access point (WAP)** is a Layer 2 device that bridges Wi-Fi clients onto a wired LAN.

- It translates between the 802.11 (Wi-Fi) wireless standard and 802.3 (Ethernet) wired standard.
- Clients connect wirelessly; the WAP connects to a switch over a cable.
- A WAP is **not** a router — it does not assign IP addresses or route between networks. A home "router" is usually a modem + switch + WAP + router bundled into one box.

Common misconceptions:

- **"Hub and switch are the same."** No — a hub broadcasts to all ports; a switch learns and forwards only to the right port.
- **"A gateway is just a fancy router."** Partially. The word has two meanings: in IP config it's your local router; in architecture it means a protocol translator at a higher layer.
- **"A WAP gives you internet."** No — it gives wireless access to the LAN. The router decides whether packets reach the internet.
- **"Routers and switches are interchangeable."** No — different layers, different jobs. See [nat-firewalls](nat-firewalls) for related perimeter devices.

blocks.subTitle: Switch vs router
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: What is the difference between a switch and a router?**

A **switch** operates at Layer 2 and forwards frames within one network using MAC addresses. A **router** operates at Layer 3 and routes packets between different networks using IP addresses. Use a switch to connect devices on the same LAN; use a router to connect that LAN to other networks or the internet.

blocks.subTitle: Hub vs switch
blocks.markdown:
⭐ **Q: Why did switches replace hubs?**

A hub floods every frame to all ports — all devices share one collision domain, wasting bandwidth and causing collisions. A switch learns MAC addresses and sends each frame only to the correct port, giving each port its own collision domain. Result: no collisions, much higher effective throughput.

blocks.subTitle: What layer does a router operate at?
blocks.markdown:
**Q: At what OSI layer does a router operate, and what does that mean?**

Layer 3 — the Network layer. That means a router reads and acts on **IP addresses** (not MAC addresses). It maintains a routing table to decide the best path for each packet, and it separates broadcast domains so broadcast traffic in one network does not flood another.

**Q: What is a gateway?**

In IP config, the "default gateway" is the router address your machine sends packets to when the destination is outside the local network. In architecture, a gateway is any device that translates between two different protocols — it may operate at Layer 4 through 7.
